courses.title: English Language Arts 8
courses.description: Grade 8 English Language Arts built around classic short stories, S. E. Hinton's The Outsiders, founding-era and abolition speeches, the Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, American poetry, the play The Diary of Anne Frank, Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream with its Ovidian source, and a culminating research project. Each week integrates close reading, text-based discussion, writing (narrative, argument, literary analysis, informative and research), grammar (verbals, voice and mood, punctuation) and Greek/Latin vocabulary study, plus 20–30 minutes of daily independent reading.
courses.framework: California Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts & Literacy; 2014 California ELA/ELD Framework

standards.RL.8.1: Cite the textual evidence that most strongly supports an analysis of what a literary text says explicitly and by inference.
standards.RL.8.2: Determine a theme or central idea of a text, analyze its development including its relationship to characters, setting and plot; summarize objectively.
standards.RL.8.3: Analyze how particular lines of dialogue or incidents in a story or drama propel the action, reveal aspects of a character, or provoke a decision.
standards.RL.8.4: Determine the meaning of words and phrases including figurative and connotative meanings; analyze the impact of word choice on meaning and tone, including analogies and allusions.
standards.RL.8.5: Compare and contrast the structure of two or more texts and analyze how the differing structure of each contributes to meaning and style.
standards.RL.8.6: Analyze how differences in the points of view of characters and the audience or reader (dramatic irony) create suspense or humor.
standards.RL.8.7: Analyze the extent to which a filmed or live production of a story or drama stays faithful to or departs from the text or script.
standards.RL.8.9: Analyze how a modern work of fiction draws on themes, patterns of events, or character types from myths, traditional stories, or religious works, describing how the material is rendered new.
standards.RL.8.10: Read and comprehend literature, including stories, dramas and poems, at the high end of the grades 6–8 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
standards.RI.8.1: Cite the textual evidence that most strongly supports an analysis of what an informational text says explicitly and by inference.
standards.RI.8.2: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development, including its relationship to supporting ideas; provide an objective summary.
standards.RI.8.3: Analyze how a text makes connections among and distinctions between individuals, ideas, or events (through comparisons, analogies or categories).
standards.RI.8.4: Determine the meaning of words and phrases, including figurative, connotative and technical meanings; analyze the impact of word choice on meaning and tone.
standards.RI.8.5: Analyze in detail the structure of a specific paragraph in a text, including the role of particular sentences in developing and refining a key concept.
standards.RI.8.6: Determine an author's point of view or purpose and analyze how the author acknowledges and responds to conflicting evidence or viewpoints.
standards.RI.8.7: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using different mediums (print, digital text, video, multimedia) to present a particular topic or idea.
standards.RI.8.8: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence relevant and sufficient; recognize irrelevant evidence.
standards.RI.8.9: Analyze a case in which two or more texts provide conflicting information on the same topic and identify where the texts disagree on matters of fact or interpretation.
standards.RI.8.10: Read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 6–8 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
standards.W.8.1: Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence, acknowledging and distinguishing alternate or opposing claims.
standards.W.8.2: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas, concepts and information through relevant content.
standards.W.8.3: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences using effective technique, relevant details and well-structured event sequences.
standards.W.8.4: Produce clear and coherent writing in which development, organization and style are appropriate to task, purpose and audience.
standards.W.8.5: Develop and strengthen writing by planning, revising, editing, rewriting or trying a new approach.
standards.W.8.6: Use technology, including the Internet, to produce and publish writing and present relationships between information and ideas efficiently.
standards.W.8.7: Conduct short research projects to answer a question, drawing on several sources and generating additional related questions.
standards.W.8.8: Gather relevant information from multiple print and digital sources, assess credibility, quote or paraphrase while avoiding plagiarism, and follow a standard citation format.
standards.W.8.9: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection and research.
standards.W.8.10: Write routinely over extended and shorter time frames for a range of tasks, purposes and audiences.
standards.SL.8.1: Engage effectively in collaborative discussions, building on others' ideas, posing and responding to questions, and qualifying or justifying views.
standards.SL.8.2: Analyze the purpose of information presented in diverse media and formats and evaluate the motives (social, commercial, political) behind its presentation.
standards.SL.8.3: Delineate a speaker's argument and specific claims, evaluating the soundness of reasoning and relevance and sufficiency of evidence.
standards.SL.8.4: Present claims and findings emphasizing salient points in a focused, coherent manner with relevant evidence, sound reasoning, eye contact, adequate volume and clear pronunciation.
standards.SL.8.5: Integrate multimedia and visual displays into presentations to clarify information, strengthen claims and evidence, and add interest.
standards.SL.8.6: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when appropriate.
standards.L.8.1: Demonstrate command of grammar and usage: explain the function of verbals (gerunds, participles, infinitives); form and use active and passive voice; form and use verbs in the indicative, imperative, interrogative, conditional and subjunctive mood; recognize and correct inappropriate shifts in verb voice and mood.
standards.L.8.2: Demonstrate command of capitalization, punctuation and spelling: use commas, ellipses and dashes to indicate a pause or break; use an ellipsis to indicate an omission; spell correctly.
standards.L.8.3: Use knowledge of language and its conventions, using verbs in the active and passive voice and in the conditional and subjunctive mood to achieve particular effects.
standards.L.8.4: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown words using context, Greek or Latin affixes and roots, and reference materials.
standards.L.8.5: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language (verbal irony, puns), word relationships and nuances in word meanings (connotation).
standards.L.8.6: Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases.

units.title: Short Stories: Suspense, Irony and Point of View
units.big_idea: Authors create suspense and irony by controlling what characters and readers know.

units.title: Novel Study: The Outsiders
units.big_idea: Loyalty, class and identity shape who we become, and a novel's theme grows through characters' choices.

units.title: Voices of Liberty: Rhetoric and Argument
units.big_idea: Effective arguments combine clear claims, relevant evidence and persuasive appeals while answering opposing views.

units.title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
units.big_idea: Literacy is a path to freedom; autobiography uses personal experience to argue for justice.

units.title: American Poetry
units.big_idea: Poets use form, sound and figurative language to express individual and national identity.

units.title: Drama and History: The Diary of Anne Frank
units.big_idea: Drama and nonfiction preserve memory; dramatic irony lets audiences feel the weight of history.

units.title: Myth Made New: Ovid and A Midsummer Night's Dream
units.big_idea: Writers transform ancient stories, reshaping familiar patterns for new audiences and purposes.

units.title: Research and Presentation
units.big_idea: Strong research begins with good questions, credible sources and honest citation, and ends with clear communication.

objectives: Analyze how a first-person narrator's point of view creates suspense
Identify gerunds and their functions in sentences
materials: Edgar Allan Poe, 'The Tell-Tale Heart' (Project Gutenberg)

days.title: Launch & reading inventory
days.work: Complete a reading interest survey, choose an independent reading book, and write a one-page 'reading life' reflection; read Poe's biography.

days.title: Read 'The Tell-Tale Heart'
days.work: Read the story aloud (or with the LibriVox recording) and annotate every place the narrator insists he is not mad.

days.title: Narrator reliability
days.work: Write a paragraph citing three pieces of evidence that the narrator is unreliable and explain how that builds suspense.

days.title: Grammar: gerunds
days.work: Learn that gerunds are -ing verbals used as nouns; find 5 in the story and write 8 original sentences using gerunds as subject, object and object of preposition.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a reading quiz on the story and roots (acu-, dis-, -ous); share a 2-minute oral summary using precise vocabulary.

weeks.assessment: Reading quiz plus evidence paragraph scored on claim, evidence and explanation.

objectives: Analyze how dialogue and incidents propel the plot and reveal character
Identify participles and participial phrases
materials: W. W. Jacobs, 'The Monkey's Paw' (Project Gutenberg)

days.title: Read Part I
days.work: Read Part I and list every warning given about the paw; predict what the first wish will bring.

days.title: Read Parts II–III
days.work: Finish the story and complete a plot diagram marking where suspense peaks.

days.title: Dialogue that propels
days.work: Choose 3 lines of dialogue (e.g., Sergeant-Major Morris's 'Better let it burn') and write how each propels action or reveals character.

days.title: Grammar: participles
days.work: Identify present and past participles used as adjectives; combine 10 pairs of sentences using participial phrases and fix 3 dangling modifiers.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a timed constructed response: 'How does Jacobs use foreshadowing to build dread?' and take a roots quiz on cred-, fid-, -ulous.

weeks.assessment: Timed constructed response and vocabulary quiz.

weeks.topic: 'The Gift of the Magi': irony and theme
objectives: Distinguish situational, verbal and dramatic irony
Determine a theme and write an objective summary
materials: O. Henry, 'The Gift of the Magi' (Project Gutenberg)

days.title: Read 'The Gift of the Magi'
days.work: Read the story and track each character's sacrifice and what the reader knows that the characters do not.

days.title: Types of irony
days.work: Sort 10 examples from the three stories studied so far into situational, verbal and dramatic irony; explain the effect of each.

days.title: Theme & summary
days.work: Write an objective summary (no opinions) and a theme statement for the story supported by two quotations.

days.title: Grammar: infinitives
days.work: Identify infinitives and infinitive phrases used as nouns, adjectives and adverbs; write a paragraph using all three verbal types correctly.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on irony and verbals; discuss with a family member which story's ending is most effective and why.

weeks.topic: 'The Most Dangerous Game' and narrative techniques
objectives: Analyze conflict and characterization through dialogue and action
Plan an original suspense narrative
materials: Richard Connell, 'The Most Dangerous Game' (1924, public domain)

days.title: Read Part 1
days.work: Read to Rainsford's arrival at the chateau; annotate imagery that creates an ominous mood.

days.title: Read Part 2
days.work: Finish the story; chart Rainsford's internal and external conflicts and how Zaroff's dialogue reveals his values.

days.title: Mentor techniques
days.work: Collect 5 suspense techniques from the unit (short sentences, foreshadowing, cliffhangers, sensory details, unreliable narrator) with examples.

days.title: Plan a narrative
days.work: Plan an original 2–3 page suspense story with a narrator, conflict, rising action and a twist, using a story map.

days.title: Draft the opening
days.work: Write the opening scene (at least 400 words) using a hook, sensory details and one deliberate foreshadowing clue.

weeks.assessment: Narrative plan and opening scene checked against a narrative rubric.

weeks.topic: Narrative writing workshop and unit assessment
objectives: Draft, revise and edit a complete suspense narrative
Demonstrate understanding of unit concepts on a cold-read assessment

days.title: Finish drafting
days.work: Complete the story draft with dialogue and a resolution of the conflict.

days.title: Revise for pacing
days.work: Revise using a checklist: vary sentence length, add transitions that signal time shifts, and cut slow passages.

days.title: Edit & publish
days.work: Edit for verbals, dialogue punctuation and commas; type and publish the final draft.

days.title: Read-aloud
days.work: Read the story aloud to family with expression and ask listeners to identify the twist and its clues.

days.title: Unit 1 test
days.work: Cold-read assessment on an unfamiliar short story ('The Open Window' by Saki) with irony and point-of-view questions.

weeks.assessment: Published narrative (rubric) and Unit 1 cold-read test.

weeks.topic: The Outsiders, chapters 1–3: characters and class
objectives: Analyze how the narrator Ponyboy introduces characters and social conflict
Distinguish active and passive voice

days.title: Pre-reading
days.work: Read a short article about Tulsa in the 1960s and S. E. Hinton writing the book at 16; predict conflicts from the cover and title.

days.title: Chapters 1–2
days.work: Read chapters 1–2 and start a character chart (Ponyboy, Johnny, Dally, Darry, Sodapop, Cherry) with direct and indirect characterization quotes.

days.title: Chapter 3
days.work: Read chapter 3 and write a journal entry analyzing Cherry's line 'Things are rough all over' and what it reveals about class.

days.title: Grammar: active and passive voice
days.work: Identify active and passive sentences; rewrite 10 sentences from passive to active and explain when passive is useful.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on chapters 1–3; participate in a discussion on whether the Greasers and Socs are more alike or different.

weeks.topic: The Outsiders, chapters 4–6: turning point and allusion
objectives: Analyze how the church scene and Frost's poem develop theme
Explain the impact of allusions

days.title: Chapter 4
days.work: Read chapter 4 and analyze the turning point in the park; list the consequences Ponyboy and Johnny face.

days.title: Chapter 5 & Frost
days.work: Read chapter 5 and the poem 'Nothing Gold Can Stay'; annotate the poem's imagery and connect 'gold' to Ponyboy and Johnny.

days.title: Chapter 6
days.work: Read chapter 6 and analyze the church fire as a moment that changes how characters see themselves.

days.title: Allusion study
days.work: Explain the allusions to 'Gone with the Wind' and Frost and how each deepens the theme.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a theme paragraph about 'staying gold' with two pieces of evidence.

weeks.topic: The Outsiders, chapters 7–9: conflict and consequences
objectives: Analyze how incidents and dialogue lead to decisions
Use active and passive voice for effect

days.title: Chapter 7
days.work: Read chapter 7 and analyze Randy's conversation with Ponyboy as evidence that Socs face problems too.

days.title: Chapter 8
days.work: Read chapter 8 and write about how Johnny's condition and words ('Useless...fighting's no good') affect Ponyboy.

days.title: Chapter 9
days.work: Read chapter 9 and analyze the rumble and Johnny's last words.

days.title: Grammar for effect
days.work: Rewrite a paragraph about the rumble in both active and passive voice and explain which creates more impact.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on chapters 7–9.

weeks.topic: The Outsiders, chapters 10–12: resolution and theme
objectives: Analyze how the ending resolves conflicts and develops theme
Plan a literary analysis essay with a defensible thesis

days.title: Chapter 10
days.work: Read chapter 10 and write a journal entry analyzing Dally's death and why Ponyboy refuses to accept Johnny is gone.

days.title: Chapters 11–12
days.work: Finish the novel; annotate Johnny's letter and explain how the last line's return to the first line creates a circular structure.

days.title: Thesis workshop
days.work: Draft three thesis statements answering 'What does Hinton suggest about growing up?' and choose the most arguable one.

days.title: Evidence gathering
days.work: Select 6 quotations from across the novel and write two sentences of analysis for each in an evidence chart.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Build a full outline (introduction, three body paragraphs, conclusion) and take a quiz on chapters 10–12.

weeks.topic: Literary analysis essay and film comparison
objectives: Write a multi-paragraph literary analysis essay
Analyze how the 1983 film adaptation stays faithful to or departs from the novel
materials: The Outsiders (1983 film, library DVD or streaming)

days.title: Draft body paragraphs
days.work: Draft three body paragraphs using the claim-quotation-commentary pattern with embedded, cited quotations.

days.title: Introduction, conclusion & revision
days.work: Write the introduction and conclusion, then revise for transitions and verb voice using a checklist.

days.title: Film comparison
days.work: Watch the church-fire and rumble scenes from the 1983 film and chart what was kept, changed or cut and why.

days.title: Socratic seminar
days.work: Prepare 3 open questions and discuss 'Did the film capture the novel's theme?' citing both the text and film.

days.title: Unit 2 test
days.work: Take the novel test (vocabulary, character, theme, allusion) and submit the final essay.

weeks.assessment: Literary analysis essay (rubric) and Unit 2 test.

objectives: Identify ethos, pathos and logos in a speech
Evaluate a speaker's claims and reasoning
Recognize indicative and imperative mood
materials: Patrick Henry, 'Speech to the Second Virginia Convention' (1775)

days.title: Rhetorical appeals
days.work: Learn ethos, pathos and logos and label the dominant appeal in 6 modern advertisements with a sentence of explanation each.

days.title: Read the speech
days.work: Read Henry's speech aloud and annotate rhetorical questions, repetition and each appeal in the margins.

days.title: Evaluating the argument
days.work: Delineate Henry's central claim, supporting claims and evidence in a chart and judge whether the reasoning is sound and sufficient.

days.title: Grammar: verb moods
days.work: Learn the indicative, imperative, interrogative, conditional and subjunctive moods; label 10 sentences from the speech by mood.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on rhetorical appeals and moods; deliver the speech's final paragraph aloud with deliberate emphasis.

weeks.assessment: Appeals and moods quiz; oral delivery.

weeks.topic: The Declaration of Independence and the Gettysburg Address
objectives: Analyze how the structure of a foundational document builds an argument
Analyze word choice and tone in a speech
Use conditional and subjunctive mood for effect
materials: Declaration of Independence and Gettysburg Address transcripts (National Archives)

days.title: Declaration structure
days.work: Outline the Declaration's four parts and explain how the second paragraph's sentences build from self-evident truths to the right to revolution.

days.title: Loaded words
days.work: List 10 words with strong connotations ('tyranny', 'usurpations', 'merciless') and explain how they shape tone toward the King.

days.title: Gettysburg Address
days.work: Close-read the Gettysburg Address, marking parallelism ('we can not dedicate—we can not consecrate') and the past-present-future structure.

days.title: Grammar: conditional and subjunctive
days.work: Write 8 sentences using conditional ('would', 'could') and subjunctive ('If I were', 'I insist that he be') moods for persuasive effect.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a short response comparing how each text uses structure to persuade.

weeks.topic: Women's rights voices: Sojourner Truth and Elizabeth Cady Stanton
objectives: Analyze how speakers acknowledge and respond to opposing viewpoints
Correct inappropriate shifts in verb voice and mood
materials: Sojourner Truth, 'Ain't I a Woman?' (1851, Gage version and Robinson version)

days.title: 'Ain't I a Woman?'
days.work: Read the speech and trace how each repetition of the refrain answers a specific claim made by male opponents.

days.title: Two versions
days.work: Compare the 1851 Robinson report with the 1863 Gage version and discuss why the texts differ and which is more reliable.

days.title: Declaration of Sentiments
days.work: Read the Declaration of Sentiments and chart how Stanton borrows the structure of the Declaration of Independence.

days.title: Grammar: shifts
days.work: Correct 10 sentences with inappropriate shifts in voice or mood and write a paragraph with consistent active, indicative verbs.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz analyzing a short new passage for claim, counterclaim and rebuttal.

objectives: Analyze two texts that provide conflicting information
Evaluate the credibility of sources
Evaluate a speaker's argument
materials: paired argument articles from CommonLit or ReadWorks (e.g., cell phones in schools)

days.title: Choose a debate
days.work: Read two articles on opposite sides of a teen-relevant debate and annotate each article's claim and strongest evidence.

days.title: Fact vs interpretation
days.work: Mark each place the articles disagree and label whether they disagree on facts or on interpretation of the same facts.

days.title: Evaluating sources
days.work: Apply a credibility checklist (author, date, purpose, evidence, bias) to 4 additional online sources and keep the best two.

days.title: Listening to arguments
days.work: Watch a short student debate or TED-Ed talk on the topic and evaluate whether each speaker's evidence is relevant and sufficient.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write your own claim with three reasons and note one counterclaim you must answer.

weeks.assessment: Source evaluation chart and claim statement.

objectives: Write an argument essay with a clear claim, evidence, counterclaim and rebuttal
Revise for logic and clarity

days.title: Draft introduction & body
days.work: Draft an introduction with a hook and claim and two body paragraphs, each with cited evidence and reasoning.

days.title: Counterclaim & conclusion
days.work: Draft a counterclaim-and-rebuttal paragraph and a conclusion with a call to action.

days.title: Revise
days.work: Revise with a parent or peer using a rubric, focusing on whether every piece of evidence clearly supports the claim.

days.title: Edit & publish
days.work: Edit for mood and voice shifts and comma use; type and publish with a works-cited list.

days.title: Unit 3 test
days.work: Cold-read test analyzing an unfamiliar speech (Frederick Douglass, 'The Hypocrisy of American Slavery' excerpt) for claims and rhetoric.

objectives: Determine Douglass's purpose and audience
Analyze how he connects individuals and events to expose slavery's cruelty
materials: Frederick Douglass, 'Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave' (1845, Project Gutenberg)

days.title: Background & preface
days.work: Read a short biography of Douglass and William Lloyd Garrison's preface; note why the book needed a white abolitionist's endorsement in 1845.

days.title: Chapters 1–2
days.work: Read chapters 1–2 and annotate how Douglass describes not knowing his birthday and being separated from his mother.

days.title: Chapters 3–4
days.work: Read chapters 3–4 and chart how overseers Mr. Severe and Mr. Gore are described and what Douglass wants readers to conclude.

days.title: Author's purpose
days.work: Write a paragraph identifying Douglass's purpose and intended audience with two pieces of supporting evidence.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Reading quiz on chapters 1–4 and vocabulary from the text.

weeks.topic: Douglass's Narrative: chapters 5–8, literacy and freedom
objectives: Trace the central idea that literacy is the pathway to freedom
Use commas, ellipses and dashes to indicate pauses, breaks and omissions

days.title: Chapters 5–6
days.work: Read chapters 5–6 and analyze Mr. Auld's warning that learning would 'spoil' a slave and Douglass's response: 'the pathway from slavery to freedom.'

days.title: Chapter 7
days.work: Read chapter 7 and list every strategy Douglass used to learn to read and write, including trading bread for lessons.

days.title: Chapter 8
days.work: Read chapter 8 and analyze the word choice and tone of the passage about his grandmother.

days.title: Grammar: commas, ellipses, dashes
days.work: Practice using dashes and commas for breaks and ellipses for omissions by quoting Douglass accurately in 8 sentences.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write an objective summary of chapters 5–8 and take a punctuation quiz.

objectives: Analyze the turning point in Douglass's fight with Covey
Review semester reading, writing and grammar skills

days.title: Chapters 9–10
days.work: Read the Covey chapters and analyze the chiasmus 'You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.'

days.title: Chapter 11 & Appendix
days.work: Read the escape chapter and appendix; discuss why Douglass withholds the details of how he escaped.

days.title: Semester review: reading
days.work: Review literary and informational reading skills with a practice cold read and answer key.

days.title: Semester review: grammar & writing
days.work: Review verbals, voice, mood and punctuation and plan a timed essay response.

days.title: Semester exam
days.work: Take the semester exam: cold reads, grammar items and a timed analytical essay.

objectives: Write an informative essay explaining how Douglass presents literacy as a path to freedom
Participate in a text-based seminar

days.title: Socratic seminar
days.work: Discuss 'Why was reading so dangerous to slaveholders?' citing at least three passages.

days.title: Plan
days.work: Outline an informative essay with a controlling idea, three subtopics and evidence for each.

days.title: Draft
days.work: Draft the essay, integrating quotations and paraphrases with parenthetical page citations.

days.title: Revise & edit
days.work: Revise for precise vocabulary and varied sentence openings; edit for punctuation of quotations.

days.title: Unit 4 test
days.work: Unit test on the Narrative and submit the final essay.

weeks.topic: Poetry of American identity: Whitman and Hughes
objectives: Analyze extended metaphor and figurative language
Determine theme in poems responding to one another
materials: Walt Whitman, 'O Captain! My Captain!' and 'I Hear America Singing'

days.title: 'O Captain! My Captain!'
days.work: Read the elegy for Lincoln and map the extended metaphor (ship = nation, captain = Lincoln, voyage = war).

days.title: 'I Hear America Singing'
days.work: Read the poem and analyze Whitman's catalog of workers and free-verse rhythm.

days.title: 'I, Too'
days.work: Read Hughes's response to Whitman and explain how 'the darker brother' reshapes the idea of who sings America.

days.title: Comparing themes
days.work: Write a paragraph comparing the theme of 'I Hear America Singing' and 'I, Too' using evidence from both.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on figurative language terms using an unfamiliar Whitman stanza.

weeks.assessment: Comparison paragraph and figurative language quiz.

weeks.topic: Form and sound: Dunbar, Lazarus and Frost
objectives: Compare how structure (sonnet, rhymed stanzas, refrain) contributes to meaning
Analyze sound devices
materials: Paul Laurence Dunbar, 'Sympathy' and 'We Wear the Mask'

days.title: Dunbar
days.work: Read 'Sympathy' and 'We Wear the Mask'; analyze the caged-bird and mask metaphors and the effect of the refrains.

days.title: 'The New Colossus'
days.work: Mark the rhyme scheme of the Petrarchan sonnet and explain how the turn changes the meaning.

days.title: 'The Road Not Taken'
days.work: Analyze the poem's structure and debate whether its ending is sincere or ironic.

days.title: Structure comparison
days.work: Write a comparison of how a sonnet and a rhymed lyric each shape meaning, citing two poems.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on poetic form and sound devices.

weeks.topic: Narrative poetry, recitation and original poems
objectives: Analyze narrative poetry
Recite a poem with expression
Write original poems using studied techniques

days.title: 'Paul Revere's Ride'
days.work: Read the poem and compare Longfellow's version with the historical record of April 18, 1775.

days.title: Choosing a recitation
days.work: Choose and memorize a poem from the unit; mark pauses and emphasis.

days.title: Writing poems
days.work: Write two original poems: one free verse catalog in Whitman's style and one with a rhyme scheme and refrain.

days.title: Recitation
days.work: Recite the poem for family, focusing on volume, pacing and eye contact.

days.title: Unit 5 test
days.work: Unit test with an unfamiliar poem and a portfolio of original poems.

weeks.assessment: Recitation rubric, original poems and Unit 5 test.

weeks.topic: Historical context and The Diary of Anne Frank, Act 1, Scenes 1–2
objectives: Build background knowledge of the Holocaust
Analyze how dialogue introduces characters in a drama
materials: Frances Goodrich and Albert Hackett, 'The Diary of Anne Frank' (play, library)

days.title: Historical context
days.work: Read USHMM articles on Nazi Germany and the occupation of the Netherlands and create a timeline of events from 1933–1945.

days.title: Elements of drama
days.work: Learn stage directions, acts and scenes; read Act 1, Scene 1 and note how the play opens with Mr. Frank's return.

days.title: Act 1, Scene 2
days.work: Read Scene 2 aloud with assigned parts and record what each character's first lines reveal about them.

days.title: Mediums compared
days.work: Compare a photo archive, a USHMM video and a written article about the Secret Annex; evaluate each medium's strengths.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on background and Scenes 1–2.

weeks.topic: The Diary of Anne Frank, Act 1, Scenes 3–5
objectives: Analyze how incidents and dialogue reveal character and propel action
Compare the play with diary excerpts
materials: excerpts from 'Anne Frank: The Diary of a Young Girl' (library)

days.title: Act 1, Scene 3
days.work: Read Scene 3 and analyze the conflicts between Anne and Mrs. Van Daan and Anne and her mother.

courses.title: Mathematics 8
courses.description: Grade 8 mathematics following the California Common Core sequence used by Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8. Students study rigid transformations, similarity and slope, linear relationships and equations, systems of equations, functions, volume, bivariate data, exponents and scientific notation, and the Pythagorean theorem with irrational numbers. Every week mixes concept-building tasks, practice, a hands-on or graphing activity, and a Friday check.

units.title: Rigid Transformations and Congruence
units.big_idea: Translations, rotations, and reflections move figures without changing size or shape, so congruent figures are linked by rigid motions.

units.title: Dilations, Similarity, and Slope
units.big_idea: Dilations scale figures; similar triangles explain why a line has a constant slope.

units.title: Linear Relationships
units.big_idea: A linear relationship has a constant rate of change (slope) and an initial value, and can be shown in tables, graphs, equations and words.

units.title: Linear Equations and Linear Systems
units.big_idea: Equations are solved by keeping them balanced; the solution to a system is the point that makes both equations true.

units.title: Functions and Volume
units.big_idea: A function gives exactly one output per input; volume formulas for cylinders, cones and spheres are functions of their dimensions.

units.title: Associations in Data
units.big_idea: Scatter plots and two-way tables reveal patterns of association that can be modeled and interpreted.

units.title: Exponents and Scientific Notation
units.big_idea: Exponent rules follow from repeated multiplication and let us write and compute with very large and very small numbers.

units.title: Pythagorean Theorem and Irrational Numbers
units.big_idea: In a right triangle a^2 + b^2 = c^2, and many side lengths are irrational numbers we can locate and approximate.

units.title: Putting It All Together
units.big_idea: Grade 8 tools (linear models, systems, volume, data) combine to solve open-ended real-world problems.

days.work: Solve 4 word problems, such as a coin jar with 20 coins worth $3.20 in dimes and quarters.

days.title: Unit 4 test
days.work: Unit test on linear equations and systems.

objectives: Define a function as a rule with exactly one output for each input
Identify functions from tables, graphs, mappings and descriptions

days.title: Input-output machines
days.work: Play 'guess my rule' with a family member using input/output cards, then decide which rules are functions.

days.title: Is it a function?
days.work: Classify 10 relations (tables, mapping diagrams, graphs, statements like 'a person's age -> height') as functions or not, using the vertical line test.

days.title: Function notation & language
days.work: Write statements like 'distance is a function of time' and evaluate functions from equations and graphs.

days.title: Equations for functions
days.work: Write equations for functions such as the perimeter of a square or the cost of n tickets, naming the independent and dependent variables.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz: identify functions and evaluate them from 4 representations.

weeks.topic: Representing and comparing functions; semester review
objectives: Compare two functions represented in different ways
Distinguish linear from nonlinear functions

days.title: Comparing functions
days.work: Compare a function given by a table with one given by an equation (e.g., two car rental companies) and decide which grows faster.

days.title: Linear vs nonlinear
days.work: Graph y = 2x + 1, y = x^2 and A = pi r^2 from tables and explain why only the first is linear.

days.title: Semester review A
days.work: Mixed review of transformations, similarity and slope (Units 1–3) with worked corrections.

days.title: Semester review B
days.work: Mixed review of equations and systems (Unit 4) and functions; make a one-page formula and strategy sheet.

days.title: Semester 1 exam
days.work: Cumulative semester exam covering Units 1–5 so far.

weeks.topic: Linear functions, rates of change, and graphs of situations
objectives: Model situations with linear functions and interpret rate of change
Describe and sketch qualitative and piecewise graphs

days.title: Linear function models
days.work: Build functions for situations such as a phone battery draining 8% per hour from 100%; interpret rate and initial value.

days.title: Qualitative graphs
days.work: Match 6 stories (a bike ride with a stop, a filling bathtub) to graphs and describe where they increase, decrease or stay constant.

days.title: Sketching graphs
days.work: Sketch graphs from verbal descriptions and write a story for 3 given graphs.

days.title: Piecewise linear functions
days.work: Analyze a graph of a water tank filled and drained in stages; find the rate of change for each piece.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on modeling with linear functions and interpreting qualitative graphs.

weeks.assessment: Quiz on function models and graph interpretation.

objectives: Find volumes of cylinders
Use the relationship between cones and cylinders to find cone volumes

days.title: Volume of prisms review
days.work: Review V = Bh with rectangular prisms; measure a cereal box and compute its volume.

days.title: Cylinder volume
days.work: Measure 3 cans, compute V = pi r^2 h, and check by filling with water and measuring in a measuring cup (1 mL = 1 cubic cm).

days.title: Cone vs cylinder lab
days.work: Build a paper cone with the same base and height as a can; count how many cones of rice fill the can to discover V = (1/3) pi r^2 h.

days.title: Missing dimensions
days.work: Solve 6 problems finding the radius or height of cylinders and cones given volume.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz: 6 cylinder and cone volume problems including a real-world one (a cone-shaped paper cup).

objectives: Find the volume of spheres and hemispheres
Analyze how volume changes as a function of radius or height

days.title: Sphere volume
days.work: Compare a sphere to a cylinder of the same radius and height 2r to justify V = (4/3) pi r^3; find volumes of 4 balls.

days.title: Composite volumes
days.work: Find volumes of composite solids like an ice-cream cone with a hemisphere on top and a grain silo.

days.title: Volume as a function
days.work: Graph volume of a cylinder as a function of height (linear) and of radius (nonlinear) in Desmos; compare.

days.title: Unit 5 review
days.work: Review functions and volume with a 12-problem mixed set.

days.title: Unit 5 test
days.work: Unit test on functions and volume.

objectives: Construct scatter plots from bivariate data
Describe association, clusters and outliers
materials: data from family members or an online data set

days.title: Collecting bivariate data
days.work: Measure arm span and height of at least 8 people (or use a provided data set) and organize in a table.

days.title: Making scatter plots
days.work: Plot arm span vs height by hand with appropriate scales; describe the pattern.

days.title: Describing association
days.work: Classify 8 scatter plots as positive, negative, or no association and linear or nonlinear; identify outliers and clusters.

days.title: Interpreting outliers
days.work: Explain possible reasons for outliers in a car age vs value data set.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz: build and describe a scatter plot from a 12-row data table.

weeks.topic: Lines of fit and linear models
objectives: Informally fit a line to data and judge its fit
Use the equation of a model to make predictions and interpret slope and intercept

days.title: Fitting a line
days.work: Lay a strand of spaghetti over the arm span scatter plot to fit a line; compare lines and discuss closeness of fit.

days.title: Equations of fitted lines
days.work: Write the equation of the fitted line using two points on it; interpret the slope (cm of height per cm of arm span).

days.title: Predictions
days.work: Use models to predict values (e.g., price of a used car at 80,000 miles) and judge whether the prediction is reasonable.

days.title: Residuals
days.work: Calculate how far 5 data points are from the line and decide which of two lines fits better; check with Desmos regression.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz: fit a line, write its equation and interpret slope and intercept in context.

weeks.assessment: Quiz on lines of fit and interpretation.

objectives: Construct two-way tables
Use relative frequencies to look for association in categorical data

days.title: Two-way tables
days.work: Survey 20 people (or use given data) on two yes/no questions such as 'plays an instrument' and 'likes math'; organize in a two-way table.

days.title: Relative frequency
days.work: Compute row and column relative frequencies as percents and decide whether an association exists.

days.title: Analyzing associations
days.work: Analyze 3 data sets (e.g., curfew vs chores) and write a claim with evidence from relative frequencies.

days.title: Unit 6 review
days.work: Review scatter plots, lines of fit and two-way tables with a mixed practice set.

days.title: Unit 6 test
days.work: Unit test on bivariate data.

weeks.topic: Exponent rules for products, quotients and powers
objectives: Generate exponent rules by expanding repeated multiplication
Apply product, quotient and power-of-a-power rules

days.title: Paper folding
days.work: Fold a sheet of paper in half repeatedly, record layers as powers of 2, and predict layers after 10 folds.

days.title: Multiplying powers
days.work: Expand expressions like 10^3 x 10^4 to discover a^m x a^n = a^(m+n); practice 12 problems.

days.title: Powers of powers
days.work: Expand (5^2)^3 to discover (a^m)^n = a^(mn); mix with products.

days.title: Dividing powers
days.work: Expand 7^6 / 7^2 to discover a^m / a^n = a^(m-n); solve 12 mixed problems.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz: simplify 12 expressions using exponent rules and explain one rule with expanded form.

weeks.topic: Zero, negative exponents and different bases
objectives: Explain why a^0 = 1 and a^(-n) = 1/a^n
Simplify expressions with negative exponents and products of different bases

days.title: Zero exponents
days.work: Use a pattern table (10^3, 10^2, 10^1, ...) to justify 10^0 = 1; extend to other bases.

days.title: Negative exponents
days.work: Continue the pattern to 10^(-1), 10^(-2); rewrite 10 expressions with positive exponents.

days.title: Different bases
days.work: Use (ab)^n = a^n b^n to simplify expressions like 2^3 x 5^3 = 10^3; evaluate 8 expressions.

days.title: Mixed practice
days.work: Complete a 20-problem mixed exponent card sort, matching equivalent expressions.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz: evaluate and simplify 12 expressions with zero and negative exponents.

objectives: Write large and small numbers in scientific notation
Compare quantities using powers of 10

days.title: Powers of 10 on a number line
days.work: Place numbers like 3 x 10^5 and 7 x 10^(-3) on number lines labeled with powers of 10.

days.title: Writing scientific notation
days.work: Convert 12 quantities (distance to the Sun, mass of a dust grain, U.S. population) to and from scientific notation.

days.title: Comparing magnitudes
days.work: Use powers of 10 to estimate how many times larger one quantity is (Earth vs Moon mass, a blue whale vs an ant).

days.title: Using a calculator
days.work: Read calculator 'E' notation and convert planetary data from NASA into scientific notation.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz: convert, compare and order 10 numbers in scientific notation.

objectives: Multiply and divide numbers in scientific notation
Add and subtract numbers in scientific notation and choose sensible units

days.title: Multiplying & dividing
days.work: Compute products and quotients like (3 x 10^8)(2 x 10^3) and adjust answers to proper scientific notation.

days.title: Adding & subtracting
days.work: Rewrite with a common power of 10 before adding/subtracting; complete 8 problems.

days.title: Space math
days.work: Calculate how long light takes to travel from the Sun to each planet using distance / (3 x 10^8 m/s).

days.title: Unit 7 review
days.work: Review exponent rules and scientific notation with a self-checking puzzle.

days.title: Unit 7 test
days.work: Unit test on exponents and scientific notation.

weeks.topic: Square roots and side lengths of squares
objectives: Find areas of tilted squares on a grid and relate side length to square root
Estimate square roots between consecutive integers

days.title: Tilted squares
days.work: Draw squares on a grid with tilted sides; find their areas by decomposing or surrounding with a larger square.

days.title: Side lengths as square roots
days.work: Write side lengths of those squares as square roots (e.g., sqrt 10) and estimate each between two whole numbers.

days.title: Perfect squares
days.work: Memorize perfect squares 1–225; solve x^2 = p for 10 values of p including non-perfect squares.

days.title: Estimating roots
days.work: Estimate sqrt 50, sqrt 72 and sqrt 130 to the tenth by guess-and-check squaring; check with a calculator.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz: tilted-square areas, solving x^2 = p and placing square roots on a number line.

weeks.topic: The Pythagorean theorem and its converse
objectives: Explain a visual proof of the Pythagorean theorem
Use the converse to determine whether a triangle is a right triangle

days.title: Finding a pattern
days.work: Draw right triangles on a grid, build squares on each side and record areas to discover a^2 + b^2 = c^2.

days.title: Visual proof
days.work: Cut and rearrange four congruent right triangles inside a square (the 'two squares' proof) and explain in writing why it proves the theorem.

days.title: Finding unknown sides
days.work: Solve 10 problems finding a missing leg or hypotenuse, leaving irrational answers as square roots and as decimals.

days.title: The converse
days.work: Test side lengths (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 6-7-9) with the converse; use a 3-4-5 knotted string to check a corner of a room for square.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz: explain the proof in your own words and solve 6 problems including converse questions.

Find distance between two points on the coordinate plane

days.title: Real-world right triangles
days.work: Solve problems with ladders, TV screen diagonals and ramps; measure a TV to check its advertised diagonal.

days.title: 3-D diagonals
days.work: Find the longest straight object that fits in a shoe box by computing the space diagonal; verify with a measured straw or string.

days.title: Distance on the coordinate plane
days.work: Draw the right triangle under segments between points and find 8 distances.

days.title: Mixed applications
days.work: Solve 6 multi-step problems such as walking diagonally across a park vs around it.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz: 3 real-world, 2 three-dimensional and 3 coordinate distance problems.

weeks.topic: Cube roots and rational vs irrational numbers
objectives: Solve x^3 = p using cube roots
Convert repeating decimals to fractions and classify numbers as rational or irrational

days.title: Cube roots
days.work: Build cubes of side 1–5 with sugar or snap cubes; solve x^3 = p for perfect and non-perfect cubes and estimate.

days.title: Decimal expansions
days.work: Use long division to write fractions such as 5/11 and 7/12 as decimals; identify repeating patterns.

days.title: Repeating decimals to fractions
days.work: Use the 'multiply by 10^n and subtract' method to convert 0.7777..., 0.272727... and 1.16666... to fractions.

days.title: Rational or irrational?
days.work: Sort 16 numbers (sqrt 16, pi, 0.121212..., sqrt 2, 22/7) and justify each placement.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz: cube roots, conversions and classification of real numbers.

weeks.assessment: Quiz on cube roots and the real number system.

objectives: Approximate irrational numbers to the hundredth
Compare and order irrational and rational numbers on a number line

days.title: Zooming in on sqrt 2
days.work: Use successive number lines to trap sqrt 2 between tenths, then hundredths, without a calculator.

days.title: Ordering real numbers
days.work: Order sets like {pi, sqrt 10, 3.1, 22/7, 3.15} on a number line with justification.

days.title: Estimating expressions
days.work: Estimate values like pi^2 and 2 sqrt 5 + 1 and compare estimates to calculator values.

days.title: Unit 8 review
days.work: Mixed review: roots, Pythagorean theorem, distance and real numbers.

days.title: Unit 8 test
days.work: Unit test on the Pythagorean theorem and irrational numbers.

objectives: Break large estimation problems into smaller computable parts
Use scientific notation and volume to estimate quantities

days.work: Estimate how many ping-pong balls fit in your house's living room using volume of spheres and a room measurement; list assumptions.

days.title: Fermi problem 2
days.work: Estimate how many heartbeats you will have in your lifetime and express in scientific notation.

days.work: Pick a question (e.g., how many pizzas are eaten in California per year), research a few facts and build an estimate.

Use a system to find a break-even point

days.work: Choose a small business (lemonade stand, dog walking, baking) and write a cost function with fixed and per-item costs.

courses.subject: SCI
courses.title: Science 8 (Integrated)
courses.description: Integrated Grade 8 science following the California preferred integrated model. Students investigate forces, motion and energy; gravity and the solar system; waves and information technology; Earth's history and the fossil record; heredity; and natural selection. Each week includes a hands-on investigation with household materials, data analysis, and written scientific explanations, ending with an engineering design capstone.
courses.framework: California Next Generation Science Standards (CA NGSS); 2016 California Science Framework (Preferred Integrated Model, Grade 8)

standards.MS-PS2-2: Plan an investigation showing that the change in an object's motion depends on the sum of the forces on it and its mass.
standards.MS-PS2-4: Argue from evidence that gravitational interactions are attractive and depend on the masses of interacting objects.
standards.MS-PS3-1: Construct and interpret graphical displays of data describing the relationships of kinetic energy to mass and to speed.

standards.MS-ESS1-3: Analyze and interpret data to determine scale properties of objects in the solar system.

standards.MS-LS4-2: Explain anatomical similarities and differences among modern and fossil organisms to infer evolutionary relationships.
standards.MS-LS4-3: Analyze pictorial data to compare patterns of similarity in embryological development across species.

units.title: Forces and Motion
units.big_idea: An object's motion changes only when the forces on it are unbalanced, and every force comes in an equal and opposite pair.

units.title: Energy in Motion and at a Distance
units.big_idea: Kinetic energy depends on mass and speed; energy stored in fields changes with position and transfers whenever motion changes.

units.title: Gravity and the Solar System
units.big_idea: Gravity, which depends on mass, shapes orbits, tides, and the cyclic patterns we see in the sky.

units.title: Waves, Light, and Information
units.big_idea: Waves carry energy and information; materials reflect, absorb or transmit them, and digital signals carry information reliably.

units.title: Earth's History and the Fossil Record
units.big_idea: Rock layers and fossils record 4.6 billion years of Earth and life history and reveal shared ancestry.

units.title: Heredity: Genes and Reproduction
units.big_idea: Genes code for proteins that shape traits; reproduction and mutations create variation, and people now influence inheritance with technology.

units.title: Natural Selection and Adaptation
units.big_idea: Variation plus environmental pressures change trait frequencies in populations over generations.

units.title: Engineering Design Capstone
units.big_idea: Engineers define problems, test competing solutions, and iterate using data.

days.work: Peer/parent review of CER using a rubric; quiz on energy transfer.

courses.title: U.S. History and Geography: Growth and Conflict
courses.description: Grade 8 United States history from the ideas behind the American Revolution through the Constitution, the early Republic, regional divergence, westward expansion, the Civil War, Reconstruction and the rise of industrial America. Students read primary sources every week (founding documents, speeches, letters, photographs and maps), practice historical thinking skills such as sourcing and corroboration, and write evidence-based arguments.
courses.framework: California History-Social Science Content Standards (Grade 8); 2016 California History-Social Science Framework

standards.8.1: Understand the major events preceding the founding of the nation and their significance to American constitutional democracy.
standards.8.1.1: Describe how the moral and political ideas of the Great Awakening related to revolutionary fervor.
standards.8.1.2: Analyze the philosophy of government in the Declaration of Independence, emphasizing government as a means of securing individual rights.
standards.8.1.3: Analyze how the American Revolution affected other nations, especially France.
standards.8.1.4: Describe the nation's blend of civic republicanism, classical liberal principles, and English parliamentary traditions.
standards.8.2: Analyze the political principles underlying the U.S. Constitution and compare enumerated and implied powers.
standards.8.2.1: Discuss the significance of the Magna Carta, the English Bill of Rights, and the Mayflower Compact.
standards.8.2.2: Analyze the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution and how well each implemented the ideals of the Declaration.
standards.8.2.3: Evaluate major debates at the Constitutional Convention (shared power, state-federal power, slavery, individual rights, American Indian nations) and their resolutions.
standards.8.2.4: Describe the philosophy of the Federalist Papers and the roles of Madison, Washington, Sherman, Morris and Wilson in writing and ratifying the Constitution.
standards.8.2.5: Understand Jefferson's Statute for Religious Freedom as a forerunner of the First Amendment and views on separation of church and state.
standards.8.2.6: Enumerate the powers of government in the Constitution and the fundamental liberties ensured by the Bill of Rights.
standards.8.2.7: Describe federalism, separation of powers, checks and balances, majority rule, and how constitutionalism preserves individual rights.
standards.8.3: Understand the foundation of the American political system and the ways citizens participate in it.
standards.8.3.1: Analyze principles codified in state constitutions of 1777-1781.
standards.8.3.2: Explain how the Land Ordinance of 1785 and Northwest Ordinance of 1787 transferred federal lands to private holdings, townships and states.
standards.8.3.3: Enumerate the advantages of a common market among the states protected by the Constitution.
standards.8.3.4: Understand how conflicts between Jefferson and Hamilton led to two political parties.
standards.8.3.5: Know the significance of domestic resistance movements (Shays' Rebellion, Whiskey Rebellion) and the government's response.
standards.8.3.6: Describe the law-making process and how citizens participate in and influence government.
standards.8.3.7: Understand the functions and responsibilities of a free press.
standards.8.4: Analyze the aspirations and ideals of the people of the new nation.
standards.8.4.1: Describe the country's landscapes, political divisions and territorial expansion under the first four presidents.
standards.8.4.2: Explain the policy significance of famous speeches (Washington's Farewell Address, Jefferson's 1801 Inaugural, J. Q. Adams's 1821 address).
standards.8.4.3: Analyze the rise of capitalism and related conflicts (the National Bank, early Supreme Court decisions on contracts).
standards.8.4.4: Discuss daily life, art, music and literature of early national America (Washington Irving, James Fenimore Cooper).
standards.8.5: Analyze U.S. foreign policy in the early Republic.
standards.8.5.1: Understand the causes, consequences, major battles and leaders of the War of 1812.
standards.8.5.2: Know changing U.S. boundaries and relations with Mexico, Canada and Europe, including the Monroe Doctrine.
standards.8.5.3: Outline major treaties with American Indian nations under the first four presidents and their outcomes.
standards.8.6: Analyze the divergent paths of the American people from 1800 to the mid-1800s, with emphasis on the Northeast.
standards.8.6.1: Discuss the influence of industrialization and technology on the Northeast and human modification of the landscape.
standards.8.6.2: Outline obstacles and factors in building roads, canals and railroads (Henry Clay's American System).
standards.8.6.3: List reasons for immigration from Northern Europe and describe the growth of cities (Irish Famine).
standards.8.6.4: Study the lives of free Black Americans in the North who founded schools and churches.
standards.8.6.5: Trace the development of American education, including Horace Mann's campaign for free public schools.
standards.8.6.6: Examine the women's rights movement (Stanton, Fuller, Mott, Anthony).
standards.8.6.7: Identify themes in American art, transcendentalism and individualism (Emerson, Thoreau, Melville, Alcott, Hawthorne, Longfellow).
standards.8.7: Analyze the divergent paths of the American people in the South from 1800 to the mid-1800s.
standards.8.7.1: Describe the South's agrarian economy, cotton-producing states, and the significance of cotton and the cotton gin.
standards.8.7.2: Trace the origins and development of slavery, its effects, and strategies to overturn or preserve it (Nat Turner, Denmark Vesey).
standards.8.7.3: Examine white Southern society and how the physical environment influenced conditions before the Civil War.
standards.8.7.4: Compare the lives and opportunities of free Black people in the North and in the South.
standards.8.8: Analyze the divergent paths of the American people in the West from 1800 to the mid-1800s.
standards.8.8.1: Discuss Andrew Jackson's election, Jacksonian democracy, and his actions (spoils system, Bank veto, Indian removal).
standards.8.8.2: Describe westward expansion and Manifest Destiny (Lewis and Clark, Trail of Tears, Great Plains settlement, territorial acquisitions).
standards.8.8.3: Describe the role of pioneer women and the new status western women achieved.
standards.8.8.4: Examine the importance of the great rivers and struggles over water rights.
standards.8.8.5: Discuss Mexican settlements, cultural traditions, attitudes toward slavery, land-grant system and economies.
standards.8.8.6: Describe the Texas War for Independence and the Mexican-American War and their effects, including on Mexican Americans today.
standards.8.9: Analyze the early and steady attempts to abolish slavery and realize the ideals of the Declaration of Independence.
standards.8.9.1: Describe leaders of the abolition movement (Douglass, Garrison, Tubman, John Brown, Weld, J. Q. Adams).
standards.8.9.2: Discuss the abolition of slavery in early state constitutions.
standards.8.9.3: Describe the significance of the Northwest Ordinance for education and banning slavery north of the Ohio River.
standards.8.9.4: Discuss the slavery issue raised by Texas annexation and California's admission as a free state in the Compromise of 1850.
standards.8.9.5: Analyze states' rights doctrine, the Missouri Compromise, Wilmot Proviso, Compromise of 1850, Kansas-Nebraska Act, Dred Scott decision and Lincoln-Douglas debates.
standards.8.9.6: Describe the lives of free Black people and the laws that limited their freedom and opportunities.
standards.8.10: Analyze the multiple causes, key events, and complex consequences of the Civil War.
standards.8.10.1: Compare interpretations of state and federal authority in the writings of Daniel Webster and John C. Calhoun.
standards.8.10.2: Trace boundaries and geographic and economic differences between North and South.
standards.8.10.3: Identify constitutional issues posed by nullification and secession.
standards.8.10.4: Discuss Lincoln's presidency and writings (House Divided, Gettysburg Address, Emancipation Proclamation, inaugural addresses).
standards.8.10.5: Study leaders and soldiers on both sides, including Black soldiers and regiments.
standards.8.10.6: Describe major battles, geographic advantages, technology, and Lee's surrender at Appomattox.
standards.8.10.7: Explain how the war affected combatants, civilians, the environment and future warfare.
standards.8.11: Analyze the character and lasting consequences of Reconstruction.
standards.8.11.1: List the original aims of Reconstruction and its effects on political and social structures.
standards.8.11.2: Identify push-pull factors in the movement of freedpeople to Northern cities and the West (Buffalo Soldiers).
standards.8.11.3: Understand the Freedmen's Bureau and restrictions on freedpeople, including segregation and Jim Crow laws.
standards.8.11.4: Trace the rise of the Ku Klux Klan and its effects.
standards.8.11.5: Understand the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments and their connection to Reconstruction.
standards.8.12: Analyze the transformation of the American economy and changing social and political conditions in response to the Industrial Revolution.
standards.8.12.1: Trace patterns of agricultural and industrial development related to climate, resources, markets and trade.
standards.8.12.2: Identify reasons for federal Indian policy and the wars with American Indians and their link to development.
standards.8.12.3: Explain how governments encouraged business expansion through tariffs, banking, land grants and subsidies.
standards.8.12.4: Discuss entrepreneurs, industrialists and bankers (Carnegie, Rockefeller, Leland Stanford).
standards.8.12.5: Examine the effects of urbanization, renewed immigration and industrialization, including the conservation movement.
standards.8.12.6: Discuss child labor, working conditions, laissez-faire policy and the labor movement (Samuel Gompers).
standards.8.12.7: Identify new sources of immigration, immigrant contributions, assimilation, and nativism.
standards.8.12.8: Identify the characteristics and impact of Grangerism and Populism.
standards.8.12.9: Name significant inventors and inventions (Edison, Bell, the Wright brothers) and how they improved life.

units.title: Roots of Revolution and the Declaration
units.big_idea: Enlightenment and English traditions inspired colonists to claim natural rights and declare independence.

units.title: Creating the Constitution
units.big_idea: The framers replaced a weak confederation with a Constitution balancing power, rights and compromise, including compromises over slavery.

units.title: Launching the New Nation
units.big_idea: Early leaders turned the Constitution into a working government, sparking party conflict and debates about national identity.

units.title: Foreign Policy and the Industrializing Northeast
units.big_idea: The young nation asserted itself abroad while the Northeast industrialized and reformers pushed for change.

units.title: The South and Slavery
units.big_idea: Cotton made slavery central to the Southern economy, while enslaved people resisted in many ways.

units.title: Jacksonian Democracy and Westward Expansion
units.big_idea: Expanding democracy and Manifest Destiny drove growth that came at great cost to American Indians and Mexico.

units.title: Abolition and the Road to Civil War
units.big_idea: Reform movements and failed compromises over slavery's expansion split the nation.

units.title: The Civil War
units.big_idea: The war to preserve the Union became a war to end slavery, transforming the nation.

units.title: Reconstruction

courses.title: Spanish 1B
courses.description: Spanish 1B completes Spanish I, continuing directly from Spanish 1A and moving students from Novice Mid toward Novice High. Students order in restaurants, describe their homes and chores, shop for clothing, and begin narrating in the past with the preterite, then discuss vacations, community service, movies, and technology. New structures include venir, ser vs. estar, comparisons, stem-changing verbs, tú commands, the present progressive, demonstratives, direct and indirect object pronouns, gustar-like verbs, and saber vs. conocer. Together with Spanish 1A it prepares students for Spanish II in grade 9.

standards.WL-COMM1-NH: Interpretive communication (Novice High): understand and infer meaning from simple authentic oral, written, and signed texts on familiar topics.
standards.WL-COMM2-NH: Interpersonal communication (Novice High): exchange information in conversations on familiar topics using phrases and simple sentences, asking and answering questions.
standards.WL-COMM3-NH: Presentational communication (Novice High): present information on familiar topics using simple sentences in speaking and writing.
standards.WL-CULT1-NM: Cultures (Novice Mid): identify products and practices of Spanish-speaking cultures and compare them with one's own.
standards.WL-CULT1-NH: Cultures (Novice High): identify and describe products and practices of Spanish-speaking cultures and relate them to perspectives.
standards.WL-CULT2-NH: Intercultural interaction (Novice High): use culturally appropriate language and behavior in familiar everyday situations.
standards.WL-STRUC1-NM: Structures (Novice Mid): use agreement, comparisons, stem-changing verbs, commands, and the present progressive to communicate.
standards.WL-STRUC1-NH: Structures (Novice High): use the preterite, object pronouns, and gustar-like verbs to communicate at the Novice High level.
standards.WL-CONN1-NM: Connections (Novice Mid): use Spanish to reinforce knowledge of other disciplines such as math and geography.
standards.WL-CONN1-NH: Connections (Novice High): use Spanish to build knowledge in geography, history, and media literacy.

units.title: En el restaurante
units.big_idea: Dining out connects food, courtesy, and culture; ser vs. estar sharpens description.

units.title: Mi casa y los quehaceres
units.big_idea: Describing and comparing homes and chores introduces stem-changers, commands, and actions in progress.

units.title: La ropa y las compras
units.big_idea: Shopping requires preferences, prices, and pointing things out, in stores and markets.

units.title: ¿Qué compraste? The Preterite Begins
units.big_idea: The preterite lets us tell what we did; object pronouns make speech efficient.

units.title: De vacaciones

units.title: Ayudamos en la comunidad

units.title: El cine y la televisión

units.title: La tecnología
